concepts.name: CSRF protection in OAuth: `state` or PKCE
Top-N per group with window functions

questions.prompt: An agent config is `{"model": "m1", "tools": ["search", "code"], "temperature": 0.2}`. A client sends `PATCH` with `Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json` and body `{"tools": ["search"], "temperature": null}`. What is the result?

choices.text: `{"model": "m1", "tools": ["search", "code"], "temperature": null}`
`{"model": "m1", "tools": ["search", "code"]}`
`{"model": "m1", "tools": ["search"], "temperature": null}`
`{"model": "m1", "tools": ["search"]}`

questions.explanation: In JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396), a member set to `null` removes that member from the target, and any non-object value, including an array, replaces the target's value whole. So `temperature` is deleted and `tools` becomes `["search"]`; arrays are never merged element by element. `model` isn't in the patch, so it stays.

sources.title: RFC 7396: JSON Merge Patch
sources.claim: In a merge patch, null values indicate removal of existing values in the target; it is not possible to patch part of a target that is not an object, such as some values in an array, so arrays are replaced whole; the media type is application/merge-patch+json.

questions.prompt: Your agent's web app uses the OAuth authorization code flow. Under RFC 9700, when may it rely on PKCE instead of `state` to protect its redirect URI against CSRF?

choices.text: Never, since PKCE only protects the code and `state` is still required
Only once it has made sure the authorization server supports PKCE
Only when it is a confidential client that holds a client secret
Always, because every OAuth 2.0 server must support PKCE by now

questions.explanation: RFC 9700 says PKCE gives the same CSRF protection as a `state` value bound to the user's session, and even holds up when an attacker can read the authorization response. But the client MUST first ensure the authorization server supports PKCE; if it doesn't, `state` or the OpenID Connect nonce MUST be used. Being confidential has nothing to do with it.

sources.title: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
sources.claim: The long-established CSRF countermeasure is a random state value linking the request to the user agent session; PKCE or the OpenID Connect nonce provides the same protection, but clients MUST ensure the authorization server supports PKCE before relying on it, otherwise state or nonce MUST be used.

questions.prompt: From `conversations(id, user_id, title, created_at)` you need each user's 3 most recent conversations. Describe the query, and explain why `GROUP BY` can't do it and why you can't filter the window function in `WHERE`.

model_answer.summary: Number each user's conversations with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` in a subquery, then keep rows numbered 1 to 3 in the outer query.
key_points: Use `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` to number each user's conversations from newest to oldest
Filter on that number (`<= 3`) in an outer query or CTE, because window functions are allowed only in the select list and `ORDER BY`, not in `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` or `HAVING`
`GROUP BY` collapses each group into one output row, while a window function keeps every row and adds a value computed over its partition

questions.explanation: Window functions run after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, so their results don't exist yet when those clauses are evaluated; that is why the filter goes one level up. Adding a tiebreaker such as `id` to the window's `ORDER BY` makes the result deterministic when two conversations share a timestamp.

sources.title: 3.5. Window Functions
sources.claim: Window functions compute across related rows without grouping them into one output row; they are permitted only in the SELECT list and ORDER BY, not in WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING, so to filter on them you use a sub-select, for example row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY depname ORDER BY salary DESC) with WHERE pos < 3 outside.

questions.prompt: Your API accepts `PATCH` bodies as JSON Merge Patch (`application/merge-patch+json`). Explain how a merge patch is applied, and what it can't express.

model_answer.summary: A merge patch looks like the document: members it names are replaced, `null` removes a member, and non-object values such as arrays replace the old value whole; so it can't edit part of an array or set a value to `null`.
key_points: Members present in the patch replace the target's values, nested objects are merged recursively, and members not mentioned are left alone
A member set to `null` removes that member, so a merge patch can't set a value to an explicit `null`
Arrays and other non-object values replace the target's value whole, so you can't add or remove one array element
It suits documents built mostly from objects that don't rely on explicit nulls; use a different patch format otherwise

questions.explanation: Merge Patch is popular because the patch looks like the resource. The tempting assumption is that arrays merge like objects; they don't, so a client that sends one array item wipes the others. Fields where `null` has meaning also can't be set through it.

sources.title: RFC 7396: JSON Merge Patch
sources.claim: Null values in a merge patch indicate removal; non-object values, including arrays, replace the target value whole, so part of an array can't be patched; the format suits documents that primarily use objects and do not make use of explicit null values.

questions.prompt: An attacker makes a victim's browser load your OAuth client's redirect URI with an authorization code from the attacker's own account. What is this attack, and what has long stopped it?

choices.text: CSRF; a random `state` value bound to the user's browser session
Code interception; a client secret shipped inside the browser app
Token replay; rotating the refresh token on every token refresh
Clickjacking; an `X-Frame-Options` header on the sign-in page

questions.explanation: Injecting a request into the client's redirect URI so the victim's session uses the attacker's resources is the CSRF variant RFC 9700 describes. The long-established fix is a random `state` value that ties the redirect to the user agent session that started the flow; PKCE or the OIDC nonce gives the same protection. A secret in a browser app isn't secret, and refresh token rotation solves a different problem.

sources.title: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
sources.claim: An attacker injecting a request to the redirection URI of the legitimate client on the victim's device, for example to make the client access resources under the attacker's control, is a CSRF variant; the long-established countermeasure is a random CSRF token in the state parameter linking the request to the user agent session.

questions.prompt: What does `SELECT id, user_id, count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) FROM conversations` return?

choices.text: One row per user, with the number of conversations that user has
An error, because `count(*)` needs a `GROUP BY user_id` clause too
Every conversation row, each with its user's conversation count
Every conversation row, each with a running count up to that row

questions.explanation: A window function keeps every input row and adds a value computed over the row's partition. With `PARTITION BY` and no `ORDER BY`, the frame is the whole partition, so each row shows its user's total. A running count would need an `ORDER BY` inside `OVER`; one row per user is what `GROUP BY` does.

sources.title: 3.5. Window Functions
sources.claim: A window function does not group rows into a single output row, so each row keeps its identity; without ORDER BY in the window the frame is all rows of the partition, while with ORDER BY it runs from the partition start to the current row.

questions.prompt: From `conversations(id, user_id, title, created_at)` you need each user's 3 most recent conversations, using `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)`. Which of these are true in PostgreSQL? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Filter on the row number in an outer query or CTE, e.g. `WHERE rn <= 3`
Put `row_number() OVER (...) <= 3` straight into the query's `WHERE`
A window function keeps every row, unlike `GROUP BY`, which merges them
Window functions run after `WHERE`, so they can't be filtered there
`GROUP BY user_id` with `LIMIT 3` returns three rows for each user

questions.explanation: Window functions are allowed only in the select list and `ORDER BY`, because they logically run after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING` (d), so you compute the row number in a sub-select and filter it outside (a), not in the same `WHERE` (b). Unlike `GROUP BY`, which collapses each group into one row, a window function keeps every row (c). `LIMIT` caps the whole result, not each group, and `GROUP BY` gives one row per user anyway (e).

sources.title: 3.5. Window Functions
sources.claim: Window functions don't group rows into one output row; they are permitted only in the SELECT list and ORDER BY, not in WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING, because they logically execute after those clauses, so filtering on them uses a sub-select such as row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY depname ORDER BY salary DESC) with WHERE pos < 3 outside.

questions.prompt: Your API accepts `PATCH` bodies as JSON Merge Patch (`application/merge-patch+json`, RFC 7396). Which of these are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A member set to `null` in the patch removes that member from the target
An array in the patch is merged element by element into the target's array
Members the patch doesn't mention are left as they are in the target
Setting a field to `null` explicitly is done by sending `null` for it
An array in the patch replaces the target's array as a whole

questions.explanation: A merge patch looks like the document it changes: `null` means remove the member (a), so you can't use it to store an explicit `null` (d). Members the patch doesn't name are untouched (c), and nested objects are merged recursively. Arrays and other non-object values replace the target value whole (e), so you can't add or remove one array element (b).

sources.title: RFC 7396: JSON Merge Patch
sources.claim: Null values in a merge patch indicate removal of existing values; content the patch doesn't mention is left untouched; non-object values such as arrays replace the target value whole, so arrays can't be partly changed; merge patch suits documents that primarily use objects and don't use explicit null values.
